channel.title: Genomics Feed
channel.description: Aggregated research articles from Nature Genetics, Cell Genomics, Genome Biology, Genome Research, Nucleic Acids Research, and RNA.

item.title: Cell Genomics: Amyloid and tau display distinct patterns across Alzheimer’s in anterior caudate
item.description: Kana et al. built a single-nucleus and spatial atlas of the anterior caudate across Alzheimer’s disease. Caudate pathology is mainly diffuse amyloid-β plaques and white matter tau threads. Despite no neuronal loss, they find an increase in FLT1+/IL1B+ microglial state with vascular signaling and altered gene expression in fast-spiking interneurons.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Saturation genome editing of BRCA1 across cell types improves interpretation of variant pathogenicity
item.description: Saturation genome editing maps the functional effects of thousands of BRCA1 variants across two complementary cell models. Discordantly scored variants reflect the importance of context and provide insights for improving BRCA1 variant interpretation.

item.title: Cell Genomics: Genome-wide association study meta-analysis identifies susceptibility loci informing Ewing sarcoma etiology and potential mechanisms of risk
item.description: Hubbard et al. perform a genome-wide association meta-analysis combined with a case-parent trio study to identify 14 Ewing sarcoma susceptibility loci. Most loci contain GGAA microsatellites bound by the tumor-defining EWSR1::FLI1 fusion protein, highlighting interplay between inherited genetic variation and somatically acquired oncogenic fusions in Ewing sarcoma.

item.title: Genome Biology: Spatial transcriptomics defines segmental and temporal dynamics of pig intestinal epithelium
Nucleic Acids Research: RNA sequencing depth guidelines for the study of alternative splicing
item.description: Abstract A key parameter in the experimental design of RNA-seq projects is the choice of sequencing depth. Considering a limited budget, one needs to find a trade-off between the number of samples and the sensitivity of the analysis, particularly concerning lowly expressed genes. While previous studies have proposed a lower bound for the comprehensive analysis of differential gene expression, for the analysis of alternative splicing, it has only been proposed for human adipose tissue. However, alternative splicing differs across tissues and conditions. We analyzed publicly available and newly generated deep-sequenced paired-end RNA-seq samples (between 150 and >500 million reads, read length 50–150 bp) from human buffy coat cells and diverse sets of tissues, including gluteal subcutaneous fat, heart, and hypothalamus. Our results show that the sequencing depth typically used in published cohorts is not sufficient to comprehensively capture the landscape of alternative splicing. This motivates the use of deeper sequencing or long-read technologies in future studies. Toward this goal, we offer guidelines and a website ( https://sequencing-depth4splicing.com/ ) for choosing a suitable sequencing depth.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: The balance between R-loops and RNAPII occupancy determines the outcome of transcription–replication conflicts
item.description: Abstract Maintaining genome integrity requires the precise coordination of replication and transcription. While R-loops are known to cause transcription–replication conflicts (TRCs), the precise nature of the barrier, whether it is the RNA:DNA hybrid itself, the stalled RNA Polymerase II (RNAPII), or a combination of both, remains elusive. Using live-cell imaging in yeast to monitor a single R-loop prone locus in real time, we demonstrate that wild-type replisomes traverse R-loop enriched transcription units with high efficiency. We find that while R-loops initially repress transcription, replisome passage prompts a robust recovery of transcription activity. Indeed, we discover that R-loops serve a critical regulatory function by suppressing excessive RNAPII occupancy. In an RNAPII mutant with high DNA affinity, the enzymatic removal of R-loops leads to a pile-up of RNAPII molecules, creating a barrier to replication, more severe than the R-loops themselves. Thus, our findings reveal a dual nature of R-loops: while they can be obstacles and repress transcription, they can also serve as a physiological buffer that prevents the formation of high-density RNAPII ‘trains’. These findings establish that the precise regulation of both R-loop levels and RNAPII density is critical for preventing harmful TRCs and maintaining genome stability.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Truncated APC regulates alternative splicing by interacting with DDX21 in colorectal cancer
item.description: Abstract Truncating mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene—a key driver of colorectal cancer (CRC) initiation—frequently lead to the production of a truncated APC protein (Trunc-APC). However, its post-transcriptional roles and oncogenic potential remain largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that Trunc-APC functions as an RNA-binding protein, directly associating with pre-mRNA via its N-terminal 1–169 amino acid region to regulate widespread alternative splicing (AS) in CRC cells. Specifically, Trunc-APC promotes exon inclusion in ARHGEF11 , producing an oncogenic isoform that is associated with enhanced Bcl-xL/BAX complex formation and reduced apoptosis. Mechanistically, Trunc-APC interacts with the RNA helicase DDX21 and facilitates SF3B complex recruitment to pre-mRNA, thereby modulating splicing patterns. Notably, treatment with the splicing inhibitor Madrasin significantly reduced tumor burden in ApcMin/+ CRC mice, indicating strong antitumor efficacy. Collectively, these findings establish Trunc-APC as a novel regulator of alternative splicing and a promoter of CRC progression, and highlight the therapeutic potential of targeting the Trunc-APC/DDX21/SF3B axis in CRC.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: A RARγ–SMARCA5 chromatin-remodeling axis stabilizes AR luminal programs and opposes lineage plasticity in prostate cancer
item.description: Abstract In prostate cancer (PCa), epigenomic mechanisms drive resistance to androgen receptor (AR) signaling inhibitors, such as enzalutamide (enza). We tested whether retinoic acid receptor gamma (RARγ) shapes the epigenome to direct AR transcription, promote luminal identity, and limit enza resistance. RARγ restoration in enza-resistant 22Rv1 cells induced a large RARγ complex containing its coactivator TACC1 and the chromatin remodeler ISWI ATPase SMARCA5. RARγ restoration expanded and redistributed the AR cistrome toward active promoters, enhancers, and unique super-enhancers and increased the overlap with H3K27ac. RARγ restoration also increased SMARCA5 promoter-proximal binding that overlapped with G 2 /M-enriched AR cistrome, linking AR redistribution to cell cycle-associated chromatin engagement, including at luminal genes. In 22Rv1 and LNCaP C4-2 (also enza-resistant), RARγ restoration directed the AR transcriptome toward luminal differentiation. A miR-96 antagomir (targeting RARγ) mirrored the impact of RARγ restoration. RARγ antagonized the actions of the master lineage regulator ONECUT2 at the cistrome and transcriptome level and these antagonized genes were significantly associated with alternative lineages in murine PCa models of lineage plasticity and enza responsiveness and lineage plasticity in human PCa cohorts. These findings identify RARγ as a regulator of a chromatin remodeling mechanism that sustains luminal AR programs and opposes therapeutic resistance.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Bipartite DNA-binding domain of transcription factor BCL11B binds clustered short DNA sequence motifs
item.description: Abstract B-cell leukemia/lymphoma 11B (BCL11B), despite its name, is a key regulator of T-cell development, lineage specification, and T-cell malignancies. BCL11B contains a bipartite DNA-binding domain composed of two C2H2 zinc finger arrays: low-affinity ZF2-3 and high-affinity ZF4-6. These arrays recognize similar six-nucleotide motifs, TG( n )CC( n ), as seven of the eight DNA base-contacting residues are conserved between them. The most conserved interactions involve the central GG dinucleotides, recognized by arginine and lysine residues at the key base-interacting positions of ZF3 and ZF5. We determined eight crystal structures of ZF2-3 bound to 12- or 20-base pair DNA duplexes containing either one or two binding motifs. The structures reveal that ZF2-3 recognizes DNA with remarkable configurational flexibility, binding motifs on either the same or opposite DNA strands with variable spacing in three relative orientations: head-to-tail (or tail-to-head), head-to-head, and tail-to-tail. Analysis of BCL11B ChIP-seq peaks revealed a strong enrichment of 1-bp-spaced, same-orientation TGACC( c/t ) motif pairs. We also examined six neurodevelopmental disorder-associated missense variants affecting DNA base-contacting residues. Substitutions that replace bulky, positively charged arginine or lysine with smaller or hydrophobic amino acids weaken DNA-binding affinity and specificity, whereas substitutions between asparagine and lysine alter base recognition preferences.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Strand-displacement amplification reduces structure-induced PCR bias and preserves structurally diverse aptamers during SELEX
item.description: Abstract Stable secondary structures are important for aptamer folding and target recognition, but they can introduce structure-dependent amplification bias during Systematic Evolution of Ligands by Exponential Enrichment (SELEX), with G-quadruplexes (G4s) representing the most demanding case. Here, we introduce strand-displacement SELEX (SD-SELEX), which employs a polymerase with robust 5′→3′ strand-displacement activity to improve the amplification of structured templates. Comparative analyses showed that SD polymerase efficiently amplified hairpin- and G4-forming templates, whereas Taq polymerase exhibited structure-dependent amplification variability. In parallel thrombin SELEX experiments, SD-SELEX achieved 37-fold greater structural preservation and 65-fold higher batch-to-batch reproducibility than Taq-SELEX over 11 rounds. High-throughput sequencing further showed that SD-SELEX maintained G4 motif representation and progressively enriched the known 15-mer thrombin-binding aptamer through round 8, after which it was gradually replaced by newly identified G4 variants, whereas Taq-SELEX progressively depleted these sequences. SD-SELEX also identified novel G4 aptamers with affinities comparable to that of the reference aptamer, whereas representative Taq-SELEX candidates generally showed weaker binding. A parallel selection against VEGF-165 showed the same divergence, with SD-SELEX retaining structurally complex sequences and a previously reported functional motif that were progressively lost under Taq. Thus, SD-SELEX primarily improves aptamer discovery by reducing structure-induced amplification bias and preserving structurally diverse functional candidates, rather than by substantially increasing affinity alone.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Efficient count-based models improve power and robustness for large-scale single-cell eQTL mapping
item.description: This study presents jaxQTL, an efficient count-based pseudobulk single-cell eQTL mapping framework. When applied to OneK1K data, jaxQTL discovers more eGenes than existing methods while running faster.

item.title: Genome Biology: Short-read sequencing benchmarking with donor-specific assemblies
Nucleic Acids Research: Cell-free expression and NGS-powered substrate profiling reveal a thermostable metagenomic meganuclease from an extreme environment with novel specificity
item.description: Abstract As an alternative to historical enzyme isolation, metagenomic databases (e.g. MGnify) provide information on vast unculturable microbial diversity, including extreme environments, and constitute an enormous source of functional proteins. Conservative mining of these data by close sequence homology alone tends to identify merely different versions of known enzymes. Here we present a discovery strategy for meganucleases based on wider capture of less homologous enzymes in metagenomic databases, and incorporating metadata with their homology. We use cell-free expression to bypass host incompatibility and the need for purification, along with deep sequencing for experimental assessment of substrate specificity and cleavage pattern, thereby circumventing classical gel-based profiling. Specifically, we discovered the temperature-stable (>55°C), intron-encoded LAGLIDADG meganuclease I-MG11 that recognizes a GC-rich 17 base pair sequence to generate 4-nt palindromic 3′-overhangs—the first monomeric meganuclease to produce such overhangs. Co-folding models of I-MG11 bound to DNA provide a structural context for enzyme–DNA interactions, highlighting differences from other monomeric LAGLIDADG meganucleases (e.g. I-SceI) shaped by InDels (insertion–deletions) in the DNA-binding region that may cause specificity changes. Our strategy streamlines general bona fide identification and annotation of meganucleases, while the unique properties of I-MG11 expand the toolbox of molecular genome engineering.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Microfluidic concatemer sequencing unveils cooperative and competitive enhancer clusters in gene regulation
item.description: Abstract Chromatin looping plays a pivotal role in eukaryotic gene regulation; however, technical limitations have hindered the comprehensive characterization of higher-order interactions among genomic loci. As a result, key questions, such as whether enhancers function cooperatively or competitively at the single-molecule and ensemble levels, remain largely unresolved. Here, we present Drop-t, a novel microfluidics-based method that enables systematic profiling of higher-order chromatin architecture at both the single-molecule and population scales. We demonstrate that Drop-t is not only resistant to common ligation-induced DNA entanglements, which frequently cause nanopore clogging, but also provides greater relevance for elucidating regulatory mechanisms compared to existing ligation-free approaches. Using Drop-t, we uncovered extensive, previously underappreciated non-specific enhancer–promoter interactions (EPIs) and showed that these may influence transcriptional variability by competing with specific EPIs. Notably, we identified two major gene classes, dictator genes and leader genes, based on whether their promoters are predominantly regulated by competitive or cooperative specific EPIs, respectively. Together, our findings established Drop-t as a powerful tool for decoding the higher-order organizational principles of chromatin architecture and their impact on transcriptional regulation and variability.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Transcription factor 3 cooperates with CXXC finger protein 1 to regulate histone H3K4 trimethylation and developmental competence in mouse oocytes
item.description: Abstract During oogenesis, the establishment of oocyte-specific gene expression relies on epigenetic and transcriptional remodeling. Both histone modifications and transcription factors are crucial for the oocyte to acquire developmental competence; however, the mechanisms involved remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify transcription factor 3 (TCF3), an E-protein family member, as a key maternal regulator of oocyte developmental potential. Oocyte-specific deletion of Tcf3 results in female infertility, characterized by impaired meiotic maturation and early embryonic arrest at the two-cell stage. These defects are associated with defective maternal mRNA clearance and disrupted establishment of the H3K4me3 landscape in maturing oocytes. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that TCF3 directs H3K4me3 deposition at target gene promoters through interaction with CXXC finger protein 1 (CXXC1), the core subunit of the SETD1 histone methyltransferase complex. Importantly, this TCF3–CXXC1 interaction depends on their DNA-binding activity, highlighting the specificity of TCF3 in coordinating with CXXC1 to regulate maternal target genes, such as Pabpn1l . Together, our findings uncover a transcription factor-driven mechanism of epigenetic reprogramming that is essential for the maternal-to-zygotic transition.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Allele-selective targeting of uromodulin by antisense oligonucleotides reduces aggregates and kidney damage in a mouse model of autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease
item.description: Abstract Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (ADTKD) arises from gain-of-toxic-function mutations in the UMOD gene coding for uromodulin, the most abundant protein excreted in normal urine. Mutant uromodulin accumulates in the cells lining the thick ascending limb (TAL) of the loop of Henle, leading to intracellular aggregates, cellular stress, and kidney damage. Here, we demonstrate that an antisense gapmer oligonucleotide (ASO) designed against the representative c.553C > A (p.R185S) UMOD mutation produced allele-selective silencing of the mutant messenger RNA and protein in kidney cells. Short-term administration of a murine ASO analogue in the established Umod R186S/+ mouse model of ADTKD suppressed uromodulin and lowered tubular damage, whereas a non-targeting scrambled control was inactive. After a 4-week treatment, ASO accumulation in the Umod R186S/+ kidneys reached ∼320 000 copies per TAL cell, quantified using a sensitive splint-ligation assay. The ASO treatment suppressed premature mutant uromodulin and its toxic aggregates in Umod R186S/+ kidneys, whereas it had no effects on wild-type uromodulin in Umod +/+ kidneys. Notably, the ASO improved tubular function and decreased kidney tubulointerstitial inflammation in Umod R186S/+ mice. This work offers a roadmap for antisense therapy to treat ADTKD- UMOD and substantiates the therapeutic potential of ASOs in disorders of the kidney tubule.

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: Archaeal histones coordinate conserved DNA sequence motifs to promote CRISPR adaptive immunity
item.description: Abstract Archaea and bacteria acquire resistance to viruses by integrating fragments of foreign DNA at the beginning of a CRISPR locus. In the archaeon Pyrococcus furiosus , histones bind the leader to promote specific integration at the first CRISPR repeat. However, it remains unknown whether archaeal CRISPR leaders contain conserved DNA sequence motifs required for integration. Here, we analyze 542 archaeal CRISPR leaders found across Thermococcales and Methanococcales . We identify 36 motifs found up to 500 bps upstream of archaeal CRISPR loci. Scrambling or truncating novel motifs or histone binding sites found 100–400 bps upstream of the P. furiosus CRISPR modestly decreases integration efficiency. However, mutation of motif T2, which overlaps with the proximal histone site and is adjacent to the CRISPR, ablates both histone-mediated and histone-independent integration. Mutations tiled across T2 reveal that a pyrimidine at position −3 of the leader is required for histone-independent integration, and basepairs −4 to −19 are required for histone-mediated integration. T2 is found in most Thermococcales , and a similar sequence is found in most Methanococcales leaders, suggesting this motif may be a broadly conserved element that facilitates CRISPR adaptive immunity across taxonomic orders. These data shed light on the sequence requirements for histone-mediated DNA integration

item.title: Nucleic Acids Research: The anti-phage defense system GAPS4 is a double-edged sword that sensitizes bacteria to DNA-damaging agents
item.description: Abstract The arms race between bacteria and bacteriophages (phages) gave rise to multiple layers of antagonistic mechanisms, many of which remain unexplored. Here, we investigated the widespread anti-phage defense system GAPS4. We found that GAPS4 forms a heterotetrameric complex containing active PD-(D/E)xK phosphodiesterase domains. It is triggered upon sensing DNA damage, leading to genomic DNA degradation and cell suicide. We further demonstrated that this activation mechanism renders GAPS4 a double-edged sword, sensitizing bacteria to various DNA-targeting antibacterial agents. Collectively, our findings reveal a possible evolutionary trade-off between anti-phage defense and immunity against interbacterial antagonism.

item.title: Nature Genetics: A multi-tissue atlas of genetic regulatory effects in sheep
item.description: This study presents SheepGTEx, a comprehensive multi-tissue atlas of genetic regulatory variants derived from 6,761 samples across 51 tissues, providing insights into complex traits, population selection and domestication history in sheep.

item.title: Genome Biology: Community benchmarking of generative models for privacy-preserving synthetic bulk RNA-seq data generation
Nature Genetics: Efficient and accurate mixed model association tool for single-cell eQTL analysis
item.description: SAIGE-QTL is a framework for eQTL mapping that directly models single-cell read counts using a Poisson mixed model, achieving improved statistical efficiency and power and enabling rare variant set-based testing in the single-cell eQTL setting.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Robust fine-mapping in the presence of linkage disequilibrium mismatch
item.description: RSparsePro performs robust fine-mapping in the presence of linkage disequilibrium mismatch by coupling a probabilistic graphical model with a variational inference algorithm, identifying credible sets with higher power and coverage than existing methods.

item.title: Nature Genetics: An information-theoretic framework for inferring T cell dynamics from single-cell RNA and T cell receptor sequencing
item.description: T cells provide a unique setting for quantification of the relationship between genotype and phenotype. The authors introduce TCRi, an information-theoretic framework for this, and find mutual information to be a robust determinant of immunotherapeutic response.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Multiscale multimodal integration of spatial omics through a deep generative model with CORAL
item.description: Cross-scale spatial Omics Registration and Analysis via graph Learning is a deep generative model that integrates multiscale spatial multi-omics data using graph-attention aggregation mechanisms, enabling a comprehensive spatial analysis.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Longitudinal single-cell profiling of breast tumors highlights immune and epigenetic mechanisms associated with sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors
item.description: This longitudinal single-cell study of estrogen receptor (ER)-positive breast cancer suggests that strong estrogen signaling, ER-linked enhancers and active T cell responses could predict sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors, whereas resistance involves androgen signaling though hormone-sensing enhancer activity.

item.title: Nature Genetics: A framework for genome-wide characterization of DNA methylation and variant effect prediction
item.description: This study introduces a framework for integrating DNA methylation data across more than 90 tissues and cell types, characterizing genome-wide methylation patterns and predicting context-specific effects of genetic variants on DNA methylation and regulatory function using a deep learning model, Wreath.

item.title: Nature Genetics: AI-based precision prognostics and therapy personalization for childhood brain tumors
item.description: Stefan et al. present MANTIS, an AI model to predict individualized survival in childhood brain tumors from routine DNA methylation profiling. MANTIS may help identify patients who benefit from less intense treatment to reduce lifelong side effects.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Clonal hematopoiesis and cytopenias following CAR19 therapy
item.description: This study shows that clonal hematopoiesis expands after chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy and contributes to secondary myeloid cancers. In addition, the CAR vector frequently integrates into pre-existing clonal hematopoiesis.

item.title: Nature Genetics: A catalog of transcriptome genetic regulation in a consanguineous Middle Eastern biobank
item.description: This study reports an atlas of transcriptomic genetic effects from a Middle Eastern population biobank, revealing population-specific regulatory variants and links to clinically relevant traits.

item.title: Genome Biology: Comprehensive evaluation of antibody language models across multiple antibody design tasks
Genome Biology: Telomere-to-telomere genome of a dodecaploid desert shrub Prunus pedunculata reveals polyploidy-driven arid adaptation
Nature Genetics: Population-scale single-nucleus multi-omic profiling of skeletal muscle reveals extensive context-specific genetic regulation
item.description: Single-nucleus chromatin accessibility and transcriptome maps of human skeletal muscle identify cell-state and context-specific QTLs that colocalize with genome-wide association signals for cardiometabolic traits.

item.title: Genome Biology: Chemogenomic profiling of diverse Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains using the novel CRISPR-Cas9 markerless barcoded library BarMix
Cell Genomics: TFXcan reveals transcription factor programs driving GWAS loci
item.description: Adeluwa et al. developed TFXcan, a framework that predicts personalized transcription factor binding from genotype data across ∼700 transcription-factor-tissue pairs. Applied to PrCa risk, TFXcan identified specific transcription factors and coordinated programs of transcription factors that drive the disease at risk loci.

item.title: Genome Biology: The glutamine-aspartate metabolic tradeoff between fast growth and metabolic flexibility
Genome Biology: Urbanisation drives parallel genomic divergence across cities and bumble bee species
Genome Biology: Mitonuclear control of transcription complexes regulates tRNA splicing
Nature Genetics: High false sign rates in transcriptome-wide association studies
item.description: This study finds that the direction of effect captured by transcriptome-wide association studies is often reversed relative to the true biological mechanism, suggesting that caution is needed when interpreting these studies and using the results for downstream applications.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Near-complete assembly of wild emmer wheat unveils centromere reorganization during polyploid evolution
item.description: A near-complete genome assembly of wild emmer wheat with resolved centromeric regions across 14 chromosomes highlights subgenome-associated patterns of centromere remodeling during wheat polyploid evolution.

item.title: Nature Genetics: Establishing Polycomb regulatory landscapes in human early development
item.description: The authors profile H2AK119ub (H2Aub) in human gametes, two-cell embryos, eight-cell embryos, blastocysts and human embryonic stem cells. Their analysis provides a comprehensive view of H2Aub reprogramming and patterning during the earliest stages of human development.

item.title: Genome Research: Pangenome and transcriptomics reveal the genomic basis associated with interspecific variation of sexually dimorphic nuptial spines in moustache toads
Cell Genomics: NeoBridge: Biophysics-informed neoantigen prioritization and clonal architecture profiling in pancreatic cancer
item.description: Lana Mediavilla et al. present NeoBridge, a biophysics-informed machine learning ensemble that prioritizes immunogenic neoantigens. In pancreatic cancer, subclonal neoantigen load, not clonal load, associates with worse survival, suggesting that clonal architecture should inform vaccine target selection

item.title: Genome Biology: A new phased assembly of the Antarctic spiny plunderfish provides novel insights into the evolution of the notothenioid radiation
Genome Biology: The contribution of short tandem repeats to splicing variation in the human prefrontal cortex
Genome Biology: ROMET-RNA benchmarks and selects RNA 3D structures using multiple predictors and alignment strategies
Genome Biology: Germline structural variation involving gynecologic and breast cancers reveals polygenic signatures of tumor mutational load
Genome Biology: Commensal Lachnospiraceae bacterium mitigates colitis-induced mucin fucosylation deficits through ILC3/IL-22 axis
Genome Biology: Extensive admixture and introgression shape genetic diversity and evolutionary adaptation in indigenous East Asian cattle
Genome Biology: Dynamic landscapes of gene regulatory networks during early mammalian neurogenesis for understanding brain evolution and disorder risk
Genome Biology: Benchmarking long-read aligner-caller pipelines for structural variant detection across ten angiosperm species with PacBio high-fidelity sequencing
Genome Biology: Non-invasive genomic sampling uncovers novel connectivities and origins of confiscated gorillas
Cell Genomics: Choice of phenotype scale is critical in biobank-based G × E tests
item.description: Phenotype measurement scale has long been known to impact genetic inference, yet it is often ignored in modern studies. Costantino et al. characterize how the choice of phenotype scale affects the results of common analyses. They find that it can change GWAS hits and PGS × E interactions and influence PGS performance in specific subgroups.

item.title: Genome Biology: Poison exon splicing in the human brain provides a new paradigm for understanding and targeting neurological disorders
Nature Genetics: Clonal heterogeneity in human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and its impact on tumor progression
item.description: This study uses single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma tumors to investigate tumor heterogeneity and clonal evolution, providing a valuable resource for this aggressive cancer.

item.title: Genome Biology: Hi-C derived insulation strength predicts evolutionary conservation of topologically associating domains
Genome Research: Identity-by-descent captures shared environmental factors at biobank scale
Genome Research: Parental genome reprogramming drives allelic convergence while preserving parent-of-origin memory during human early embryonic development
Genome Research: The divergent 3D genome landscapes of aging and neurodegenerative mouse models
Genome Research: Reconstruction of contact signals from repeated elements with Hicberg
Nature Genetics: Micronuclear ecDNA constrains tumor cell fitness and is associated with favorable patient survival
item.description: Single-micronucleus sequencing and live-cell imaging of cancer cells, as well as analyses of biopsies from patients with neuroblastoma, reveal that ecDNA in micronuclei limits tumor cell fitness and is associated with patient survival.

item.title: Genome Biology: Surface proteomics reveals arginine metabolism as a vulnerability in high grade serous ovarian cancer
Genome Biology: Integrating physiological and proteomics signatures for understanding drought, salinity and alkalinity stress tolerance mechanisms in lentil
Genome Biology: Identification of regulators of aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling in human cells by genome-scale CRISPR screening
Genome Research: Temporal transcriptomics identifies trans -regulation by multiple lncRNAs in human iPSCs
Genome Research: Protein large language model–assisted one-to-one gene homology mapping in cross-species single-cell transcriptome integration
Nature Genetics: Imputation of fluid intelligence scores reduces ascertainment bias and increases power for analyses of common and rare variants
item.description: Imputing unmeasured fluid intelligence scores in UK Biobank reduces ascertainment bias and increases power for genetic analyses, improving out-of-sample polygenic score performance and identifying rare variant signals that are strongly enriched for intellectual disability-associated genes.

item.title: Nature Genetics: A heritability-optimized method for functional prioritization of rare coding variants in complex traits
item.description: This study presents RovHer, a heritability-optimized scoring method for estimating the functional impact of rare variants, which is applied to the UK Biobank to demonstrate its ability to enrich for missense rare variants that maximally explain complex trait heritability.

Genome Research: Viral haplotype reconstruction from long reads with virCHap

Genome Research: Nanopore sequencing identifies high-frequency somatic structural variations in laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma genomes
